abstract: |
  This study evaluates when partial warm starts generated by a Graph Neural Network (GNN) improve a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver's performance on Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) problems. Prior work establishes ways to supply learned assignments to solvers. Their practical value depends on the quality target, the comparison policy and the cost of preparing the start. A paired one-hour study compares a neural start, a relaxation-ranked start with matched assignment counts, and a baseline without an external start on 16 benchmark instances across three solver seeds. The analysis separates time to a common gap target from solution quality at the time limit and records solver and supervised execution costs. The neural start reached a moderate gap target sooner in aggregate on easy instances and reduced the one-hour gap on several medium instances. Its relative timing on easy instances depended on the target. A separate matched training comparison yielded a 1.831-fold whole-job speedup on four GPUs, alongside greater GPU-hour allocation and a lower F1 score. The study quantifies where neural guidance can help and what must be accounted for in judging its computational value. One solver thread, a limited benchmark sample and incomplete cold-use preparation measurements constrain the conclusions.
---
# Introduction

Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) asks which facilities to open and how to serve customers within capacity at minimum cost. A Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver searches for feasible decisions and bounds their cost.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) can learn patterns in related instances and propose values for some binary decisions. These values are partial warm-start candidates: they need not form a complete or feasible solution. The solver attempts to complete them and may repair or reject them. Supplying a candidate leaves the original constraints and variable domains unchanged.

Predictive agreement and solver performance measure different outcomes. A method can correctly predict many binary values and still supply assignments that contribute little to the search. @kibria2026feasibility report similar runtimes for learned and non-learned starts on their network-design instances. The practical value of a start also depends on the time required to construct the graph, obtain its features and run inference [@beiranvand2017].

The research question is: Can partial initial values predicted by a graph neural network (GNN) be used as warm starts for a deterministic MILP solver and improve its performance when solving Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) problems? The study examines when neural starting information helps and how the measurement boundary affects the estimated benefit. Using the CFL instances from MILPBench [@milpbench], it makes two empirical contributions. First, it compares the effects of partial starts on primal quality, dual bounds, gaps and times to common targets across instances and solver seeds. Second, it distinguishes solver time, supervised execution time and training cost, and identifies the preparation components relevant to a deployment comparison.

# Related Work

## Learning to Optimize

Learning to Optimize uses learned information to assist decisions within an optimization process [@bengio2021; @chen2022primer]. The acceleration, estimation and adaptation perspectives reviewed by @chen2024tutorial help distinguish a proposal that changes search guidance from one that replaces the optimizer. Here the network proposes candidate binary values; the MILP solver retains responsibility for feasibility and optimality assessment.

The variable--constraint bipartite representation follows @gasse2019, whose network learns branching choices. The present study adapts this representation to predict values for a partial start. This use complements broader work on graph-based combinatorial reasoning [@cappart2021].

## Learned primal guidance and partial starts

The closest precedents concern learned assignments and primal search. MIP-GNN already includes neural warm-starting [@khalil2022]. Neural Diving generates partial assignments and completes associated sub-MIPs [@nair2020], whereas Predict-and-Search explores regions around predictions [@han2023]. Prediction-guided neighbourhoods [@ding2020], local branching [@fischetti2003] and uncertainty-based reduction [@canturk2024] also use predicted structure to focus solution effort. These methods differ in what they predict and how they modify or restrict the search.

In fixed-charge network design, @kibria2026feasibility used a random forest and greedy repair to construct complete feasible MIP starts. Constraint-aware features improved predictive discrimination, but the learned starts performed similarly to repaired random and greedy starts on the tested HiGHS instances. This comparison illustrates why predictive accuracy, start feasibility and solver performance warrant separate evaluation.

Partial MIP starts supply selected variable values to the solver as a candidate. The remaining values are unspecified, and the original feasible region remains available [@gurobi2026]. Learned constraints [@qu2026], starting scenarios for another optimization setting [@goerigk2025] and nonlinear solution-generation mechanisms [@tang2024l2o] illustrate other interfaces, rather than direct experimental comparators for the present CFL population. The broader branch-and-bound literature makes the same distinction between learned components and complete solution procedures [@scavuzzo2026survey].

The comparison in this study uses three starting policies: no external start, an LP-ranked partial start and a GNN-ranked partial start. The two partial starts match the total number of assignments and the number assigned to one, allowing the comparison to focus on how the two procedures select variables under those counts. Appendix A compares the solver interfaces and identifies the cost components needed for a like-for-like comparison.

## Performance and computational cost

An improvement depends on the endpoint being compared. Earlier attainment of a quality target, a better feasible objective and a smaller terminal gap answer different questions. Comparable models, settings, stopping rules and parameter selection are therefore central to computational evaluation [@beiranvand2017]. The same requirement applies to the cost boundary: shorter solver time need not imply a shorter application once neural preparation is included. The experiments track solver performance and preparation costs separately on the same benchmark instances.

# Methodology

## Optimization model and reference labels

A CFL model couples facility-opening and customer-service decisions through capacity and demand constraints. The benchmark instances are represented in matrix form as

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_p^\star&=\min_x\; c_p^\top x+c_{p,0},\\
A_px&\mathrel{\bowtie_p}b_p,\\
\ell_p\leq x&\leq u_p,\qquad x_j\in\mathbb Z\quad(j\in I_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

The index $p$ identifies an instance. The matrix $A_p$, vector $b_p$ and row senses $\bowtie_p$ describe its constraints, and $I_p$ identifies its integer variables. The distributed files declare maximization. Maximizing the supplied objective rewards increases in a quantity that the cost-minimization formulation seeks to reduce, changing the optimization problem. The experiments therefore set the objective sense to minimization while retaining the supplied coefficients, constants, constraints, bounds and domains. This convention applies to the experiments; the archived benchmark files retain their original declarations. Appendix C documents the scope of this decision.

For binary variables, labels come from checked reference incumbents. An incumbent is a feasible solution retained by the solver, subject to the stated numerical checks. Admission verifies variable coverage, bounds, integrality, linear constraints and objective reconstruction, and requires a finite reported relative gap no greater than 10%. Labels may therefore be approximate and need not identify an exact or unique optimum. Predicting their values is a supervised-learning task, not an optimality certificate.

## From the model to a bipartite graph

A variable is represented by a variable node and a linear constraint by a constraint node. An edge joins them when the variable has a nonzero coefficient in that row, and the coefficient is an edge feature. This representation gives the GNN access to the couplings present in the MILP.

Each variable node has seven channels: objective coefficient, lower bound, upper bound, continuous indicator, binary indicator, integer indicator and captured root-relaxation value. Each constraint node has five: right-hand side, less-than-or-equal indicator, equality indicator, greater-than-or-equal indicator and a constant one. Each edge has one channel for the corresponding nonzero coefficient. Clipping and signed logarithms control the range of the encoded features; Appendix C gives the transformations.

During preparation, Gurobi solves the linear relaxation at the root of the minimization model with presolve disabled, a one-node limit, one thread, seed 42 and a 600-second limit. The feature vector comes from the first root callback that reports an optimal relaxation. The values are aligned to the original variables before preparation stops, so they describe that observed root state.

## Predictor, training and validation

The network adapts bipartite graph convolution [@gasse2019]. As described in Related Work, graph convolution uses the sparsity of the constraint matrix, shares local operations across nodes and accommodates instances of different sizes. The implementation here retains separate updates for constraints and variables and uses an output head that scores individual binary values. @fig-message-passing illustrates the two updates within one propagation cycle.

![One cycle of bipartite message passing.](figures/figure_message_passing.pdf){#fig-message-passing width=90% fig-pos="!htbp"}

In the first pass, each constraint collects messages from its incident variables. Each message includes the coefficient on the connecting edge. In the second pass, each variable receives messages from the updated constraints. This allows variables in the same constraint to influence one another through that constraint. The fitted network uses two cycles of width 32 and has 26,753 trainable parameters. Summed messages use normalization statistics fitted on the training graphs. The output head returns a logit $s_j$ and sigmoid score $q_j=\sigma(s_j)$ for each eligible binary variable. Appendix A gives the update equations and compares this design with other architectures.

Training minimizes positive-class-weighted binary cross-entropy (BCE) for each binary label $y_j$,

$$
\ell_j=-w_+y_j\log\sigma(s_j)-(1-y_j)\log(1-\sigma(s_j)),
$$

where $w_+$ is the number of zero labels divided by the number of one labels in the training data. When zeros are much more frequent, the factor increases the penalty for errors on ones so that their contribution to learning is less easily overshadowed. The sigmoid output is interpreted as a score, with calibration assessed separately [@gneiting2007].

Adam uses a learning rate of 0.001 [@kingma2015] and clips the gradient norm at 1 to limit large updates [@pascanu2013]. The serial fit underlying the frozen predictor uses one graph per update, four balanced draws per training instance per epoch and a ceiling of 100 epochs. The checkpoint is selected at the lowest validation weighted BCE. A separate validation step selects the score threshold that maximizes pooled F1. For the retained predictor, a score of at least 0.9991843104362488 produces a predicted one. This cutoff acts on the weighted model's scores; it is distinct from the solver's gap target and from the assignment budget below.

## Inference, partial starts and the three methods

For a new instance, the graph combines the model features and aligned root-relaxation values. The frozen GNN applies its learned weights to this graph and generates a score for each eligible binary variable. The inputs for this step are available before the main solve.

For $n$ eligible binary variables, the requested support budget is

$$K=\min\{n,20000,\max(1,\lfloor0.10n\rfloor)\}.$$

Here $n$ is the number of binary variables eligible for a starting value and $K$ is the maximum number of values supplied. The floor rounds 10% of $n$ down to an integer. The inner maximum allows one assignment when that floor is zero, and the outer minimum caps the budget at both $n$ and 20,000. If $n=0$, the budget is zero.

GNN-START (G) selects predicted ones first, ranked by their scores, and fills remaining places with confident predicted zeros. Variable names break ties. If no one is predicted, the policy abstains. The 20,000-value cap binds on medium instances, so their actual coverage is below 10%.

RELAX (R) ranks the stored LP values instead. If G supplies $k$ assignments including $q$ ones, R assigns one to the $q$ highest clipped LP values and zero to the $k-q$ lowest remaining values. It chooses its own indices. Its assignment count and number of ones come from G, so the cost of obtaining these counts belongs to the preparation of R. BASE (B) supplies no external start; the solver's internal heuristics remain available.

Each method starts from a fresh copy of the same model. For R and G, selected values are supplied as a candidate and other values remain unspecified. Gurobi may complete or repair the candidate before using it as an incumbent [@gurobi2026]. Candidate submission, acceptance, the first feasible incumbent and final performance are recorded as separate events.

@fig-pipeline summarizes the offline and application stages.

![Offline training and application of partial starts.](figures/figure_pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline width=87% fig-pos="!htbp"}

The top row follows the reference instances from checked labels through graph encoding, training and validation to frozen weights and a fixed decision rule. The second row follows a solve instance: its model and root values supply the inputs to inference, which produces G's candidate. R ranks the root values and matches G's $k$ assignments and $q$ ones. The bottom row links these two candidates and the no-external-start baseline B to the same solve procedure and evaluation metrics. All methods preserve the original constraints and variable domains. Appendix A illustrates how the matched assignments are selected.

# Experimental Design

## Instances and comparison populations {#sec-populations}

MILPBench supplies 90 CFL instances, with 30 in each benchmark difficulty group: easy (E), medium (M) and hard (H). Eligibility for supervised learning required a reference incumbent that covered the model variables and passed checks of bounds, integrality and constraints within recorded tolerances. The audit reconstructed the objective and required a finite solver-reported relative gap of at most 10%. This screen admitted 54 instances (30 easy and 24 medium). The learning split assigns 34 to training (63.0%), ten to validation (18.5%) and ten to predictive testing (18.5%).

@tbl-study-populations separates the learning roles from the sample used to compare solvers. Each sample was chosen for a different question.

| Population | Instances | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Training and validation | 34 training; 10 validation | Fit the predictor and select the checkpoint and decision threshold. |
| Predictive test | 10 | Assess agreement with reference binary assignments. |
| One-hour solver comparison | 6 easy; 10 medium | Compare B, R and G on the same model and solver seed. |

: Populations used for learning and solver evaluation. {#tbl-study-populations}

The first two rows partition the admitted learning sample. They require checked reference labels. The last row requires the model and, for R and G, the artifacts used to construct candidate values. It retains the six easy and four medium identities from the principal historical comparison and adds six medium instances (M5, M6, M9, M13, M20 and M26). The learning partitions remain fixed. The expanded solver sample broadens the range of instances evaluated, with prior exposure limiting its interpretation as an independent generalization test. The prospective experiment adds six hard instances (H0, H5, H10, H15, H20 and H25) to this solver sample. Their role is to test starting policies on larger problems with the frozen predictor. Appendix B documents the distinct historical cohorts, and Appendix C records the current and prospective comparisons.

## Solver protocols and repeatability

The completed one-hour experiment pairs B, R and G within each of 16 instances and each solver seed (42, 43 and 44). Each instance uses the same two prepared starts across seeds, so the seeds vary solver search with the predictor held fixed. Within a block, the solver loads three fresh model copies, and method order rotates across seeds. Each run uses one physical thread, a 3,600-second limit and a relative MIP gap target of 0.01%. Appendix C.10 gives the configuration. Each instance contributes repeated measurements. The three seeds are not three independent instances.

The prospective experimental design crosses the three starting policies and the same three solver seeds with five thread and search profiles on the 22-instance solver sample. At one thread it specifies conventional MIP. At four and eight threads it compares conventional MIP (`ConcurrentMIP=1`) with two independent searches that share the same total thread cap (`ConcurrentMIP=2`). An across-profile comparison at a fixed thread cap measures the response to the search policy. Changing the thread cap within one search policy addresses resource scaling. The prospective design supplies no observations to the results below.

Conventional Gurobi MIP is designed to be deterministic for controlled models, parameters, solver versions and hardware [@gurobideterminism2025]. Wall-clock limits can stop runs after different amounts of work [@gurobiwork2026]. The one-thread experiment precludes simultaneous MIP searches; its effective `ConcurrentMIP` value was not captured in the exported settings. For the prospective profiles, `ConcurrentMIP` selects concurrent MIP searches. The separate `Method` setting selects the continuous algorithm, including the root relaxation. A value of `-1` delegates selection to Gurobi [@gurobi2026].

## Endpoints and comparison rules {#sec-metrics}

For minimization, a checked feasible incumbent supplies an upper bound $z^P$, while a valid dual bound $z^D$ describes what may still be achievable. For finite nonzero $z^P$, relative gap is $g=|z^P-z^D|/|z^P|$. Zero or unavailable values retain their explicit states. A smaller gap can reflect primal improvement, dual progress or both; it is not synonymous with a better incumbent.

The analysis records terminal primal values, dual bounds and gaps, as well as whether and when each run first met a common quality threshold. A target that is unobserved during adequate follow-up is right-censored, not attained at the time limit. Missing observations and numerical restrictions are separate from censoring. Callback times are observed crossing times, not exact continuous first hits. A run may reach 10% gap yet remain censored for the much tighter terminal criterion.

Following the principle of comparing algorithms on the same task and stopping criterion [@beiranvand2017], the starting-policy ratio divides the time of the evaluated method by the time of its comparator. The primary ratio is $T_G/T_B$. A value below one favours G, one indicates equal observed times, and a value above one favours B. The same numerator rule applies to $T_G/T_R$ and $T_R/T_B$. Each ratio uses the same clock and an eligible common quality target. When either run is censored at that target, the comparison reports attainment and available quality outcomes. For resource scaling, speedup measures the gain from adding resources within a fixed method and workload [@cornellscaling]. At a cap of $r$ threads, speedup relative to one thread is $T_m(1)/T_m(r)$, and parallel efficiency is that speedup divided by $r$. An increase in resource speedup and a decrease in the starting-policy time ratio both indicate shorter times under their respective comparisons.

The comparisons are descriptive. For the solver-seed comparison, the analysis pairs runs by instance and seed. Fixed-budget outcomes use the latest observation at or before 3,600 seconds, or the terminal point when a solve ends earlier. Seed contrasts are summarized within instance before comparing across instances. The 48 blocks comprise repeated observations of 16 instances. The geometric mean summarizes relative times on the same cases with observed attainment. Each pair contributes equally on the log scale; the summary does not estimate total computing time.

Predictive metrics measure reference-label agreement separately. Precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is their harmonic mean. Average precision (AP) is the noninterpolated sum of precision weighted by recall increments, following @sklearnap; it differs from trapezoidal PR-AUC. Rare-positive assessment uses precision--recall measures alongside ROC-AUC [@saito2015]. The Brier score averages squared score error [@brier1950]. Expected calibration error (ECE) uses ten equal-width positive-score bins [@guo2017]. Variable-pooled metrics combine targets; parent-macro metrics average the individually computed instance values.

## Preparation, execution and resource costs

Computational performance includes attained solution quality, time reported by the solver, application elapsed time and memory. The application clock may include root capture, construction and transfer of inputs, model loading, inference and Start integration [@silva2025pascal]. The supervised attempt includes recorded process overhead. Preparation intervals are charged once, including R's dependence on G for matching. Training, queueing and orchestration have separate clocks.

The one-hour return measures solver and supervised-attempt time. Its preparation intervals do not establish a complete cold-use or amortized cost for either R or G.

UJA's dgx-dasci inventory lists eight 32-GB V100 GPUs, two 20-core CPUs and 512 GB of memory. It is not a runtime hardware probe or an allocation of all eight GPUs. The 6 Gb/s interface is an inventory specification. Appendix C separates requested, allocated and measured resources.

# Computational Results

## Complementary matched GPU training {#sec-gpu-matched}

The matched comparison asks how much elapsed time changes when the same graph-level training schedule runs on one V100 or on four V100s using distributed data parallelism (DDP). The fixed split comprises 34 training, ten validation and ten test instances. Each global update averages four per-graph weighted binary cross-entropies. The serial process accumulates four scaled gradients. In DDP, each rank processes one complete graph, then the ranks average their gradients before clipping and the optimizer step [@li2020ddp]. Both arms used seed 42, the same initial state and graph schedule, and completed 100 epochs, 13,600 graph presentations and 3,400 updates. Validation selects the checkpoint separately for each arm. Appendix B.10.2 reports the full comparison and Appendix C.7 records its configuration.

@tbl-gpu-pair separates training time, scheduler elapsed time, allocated GPU-hours and the selected checkpoints' predictive quality.

| Measure | Serial 1 V100 | DDP 4 V100s |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Physical CPU cores |4|16|
| Training loop (s) |1724.128|795.637|
| Slurm job elapsed (s) |2021|1104|
| Assigned GPU-hours |0.5614|1.2267|
| Selected epoch |99|92|
| Minimum validation BCE |0.045286|0.048772|
| Selected parent-macro F1 |0.723065|0.690597|
| Selected parent-macro PR-AUC |0.783809|0.769959|

: Matched GPU training time, allocation and selected quality. {#tbl-gpu-pair}

Loop speedup is 2.167 with 54.17% efficiency; whole-job speedup is 1.831. Assigned GPU-hours increase. Selected F1 falls 0.032468 (3.247 percentage points), exceeding the predeclared descriptive 0.02 loss margin; PR-AUC falls 0.013850. The smaller PR-AUC loss does not establish preserved predictive quality or statistical noninferiority. @fig-gpu-bce shows the unmodified loss trajectories.

![Training and validation weighted BCE for the matched serial/distributed comparison.](figures/gpu_bce_by_epoch_article_en.pdf){#fig-gpu-bce width=90% fig-pos="!htbp"}

Communication and gradient synchronization can contribute to sublinear DDP speedup [@li2020ddp]. GNN workloads can also involve irregular data movement [@zheng2020distdgl]; here each rank processes complete instance graphs. Matched global batches do not establish identical floating-point trajectories [@pytorch21numerical]. CPU and GPU allocations change together. The single pair shows an F1 loss, but does not identify its cause. These weights do not replace the CPU predictor.

## One-hour paired solver-seed comparison {#sec-pr94-results}

All 144 runs yielded terminal records. On the six easy instances, every method attained the observed 0.01% gap in all 18 instance–seed pairs. At that target, geometric mean time ratios $T_R/T_B$, $T_G/T_B$ and $T_G/T_R$ were 1.038, 1.083 and 1.043, respectively. G was faster than B in ten of the 18 pairs, but the larger slowdowns on E0 and E29 raised the geometric mean.

For the ten medium instances, B, R and G attained a 10% gap in 9, 8 and 12 of 30 runs per method, respectively. At 0.01%, only G attained the target, on M12 and M20 across all three seeds. M12 remains numerically restricted. Across the eight medium instances outside M4 and M12, the median of the instance-level paired gap differences was -2.11 percentage points for G versus B and -2.52 for G versus R. These fixed-budget differences include censored runs with observed incumbents and bounds. No medium pair reached 0.01% in both G and either comparator. The M20 results show attainment within the budget, with no observed paired time ratio. Appendix B.13 details the pair counts, numerical restrictions and supervised costs.

# Discussion

The easy and medium results answer different questions. Every easy run reached the tight target, so the observed times can be compared directly. The direction of the aggregate time contrast changes with the target: the geometric mean of $T_G/T_B$ is below one at 10% and above one at 0.01%. On medium instances the budget often expires before the tighter target. Smaller fixed-budget gaps are evidence about progress under this configuration. An incumbent and its bound can change in different directions, and an exclusive attainment does not give the comparison arm's unobserved time.

B versus G estimates the effect of supplying the full neural candidate. R matches assignment counts and class composition and selects indices from the root relaxation. It depends on G's preparation. G versus R is therefore a comparison of candidate construction under matched counts, with no independent LP-only deployment baseline. The unchanged feasible region also distinguishes the starts from restricted-search approaches [@nair2020; @han2023; @canturk2024].

# Conclusions and Future Research

The one-hour comparison does not establish a consistent advantage of G over B or R. G improved fixed-budget gap on several medium instances, and on M20 it alone reached the tight target under each tested seed. On easy instances, relative times depended on the target and instance. Neither finding establishes a general speed advantage or an end-to-end saving.

The matched DDP run took less elapsed time, used more allocated GPU-hours and yielded a lower selected F1. Interpretation is limited by the single training pair, the quality-based admission of reference labels, prior instance exposure and the one-thread solver design. Wall-time stopping and numerical restrictions on M4 and M12 also limit individual comparisons. Future work will examine whether starting-policy effects persist on harder instances and across solver resource and search profiles, and will extend the measurement of cold-use preparation costs.

Data and code availability. The [project repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/cfl-gurobi-gnn) provides code, partitions, derived outcomes and scripts for tables and figures. Original models are obtained from MILPBench. Access to intermediate data and checkpoint bytes depends on their artifact-specific availability and redistribution terms. Appendix C identifies which steps can be reproduced from public material.
